## Important comparability caveats

**1. The filings excerpted here do not contain ASM (available seat mile) data**, so the industry-standard efficiency metric — CASM / CASM-ex-fuel — cannot be computed. The only available proxy is cost as a percentage of revenue, which mixes cost discipline with pricing power and network mix (a carrier with premium/long-haul pricing looks "efficient" even at high absolute unit cost).

**2. Alaska's FY2024 is not comparable to its own prior year or to the peers on a like-for-like basis**: Alaska closed the Hawaiian acquisition on September 18, 2024, and Hawaiian's results are only included from that date, contributing $869M of revenue and a $113M net loss in the stub period [DOC: alaska_10k_note_acquisition.txt]. So Alaska's ratios blend ~8.5 months of standalone Alaska with ~3.5 months of a loss-making acquiree.

**3. Delta's revenue and expense lines are grossed up** by its refinery and other non-airline businesses, which inflates both sides of the ratio relative to pure-play carriers. All five do share a calendar Jan 1–Dec 31 fiscal year [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt].

## Cost-to-revenue comparison, FY2024 ($M)

| | Revenue | Op. income | Implied opex | Opex/Rev | Fuel/Rev | Labor/Rev | Ex-fuel opex/Rev |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Delta | 61,643 | 5,995 | 55,648 | **90.3%** | 17.1% | 26.2% | 73.1% |
| United | 57,063 | 5,096 | 51,967 | 91.1% | 20.6% | 29.2% | **70.5%** |
| American | 54,211 | 2,614 | 51,597 | 95.2% | 21.1% | 29.6% | 74.1% |
| Alaska | 11,735 | 570 | 11,165 | 95.1% | 21.4% | 30.6% | 73.8% |
| Southwest | 27,483 | 321 | 27,162 | 98.8% | 21.1% | 44.5% | 77.7% |

Source data: Delta $61,643M revenue / $10,566M fuel / $16,161M labor / $5,995M operating income; United $57,063M / $11,756M / $16,678M / $5,096M; Southwest $27,483M / $5,812M / $12,240M / $321M; American $54,211M / $11,418M / $16,021M / $2,614M; Alaska $11,735M / $2,506M / $3,588M / $570M [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt].

## Read-through

- **Delta** converts revenue to profit most efficiently: total operating costs consumed 90.3% of revenue, the lowest of the five, and it had the lowest fuel intensity (17.1% of revenue), reflecting the refinery hedge and a younger/premium-weighted revenue base.
- **United** is close behind (91.1%) and actually has the lowest *ex-fuel* cost ratio (70.5%), so on a fuel-neutral basis United and Delta are essentially tied.
- **Southwest is clearly the least efficient** in 2024: 98.8% of revenue absorbed by operating costs and a striking 44.5% labor-cost intensity, leaving only $321M of operating income on $27.5B of revenue.

Caveat repeated: this is a cost-to-revenue ranking, not a unit-cost (CASM) ranking. Southwest's short-haul, single-class network structurally carries higher cost *per ASM* than Delta's or United's long-haul networks, so the gap in true unit cost is narrower than the table implies — but its margin outcome is unambiguously the worst.

ANSWER: Delta — with total operating costs at 90.3% of revenue (vs. United 91.1%, Alaska 95.1%, American 95.2%, Southwest 98.8%), Delta had the most efficient cost structure in FY2024, though United is effectively tied on an ex-fuel basis (70.5% vs. Delta's 73.1%); note that no ASM data is available to compute true CASM, and Alaska's figures include Hawaiian only from September 18, 2024.
